Global existence and uniqueness of solutions in a chemotaxis system with density-suppressed motility, a θ−\theta-logistic source, and indirect signal production under a strong Allee effect

1,2Department of Applied Mathematics and Scientific Computing, Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee-IIT Roorkee, Haridwar Highway, Roorkee, Uttarakhand 247667, INDIA. 3Department of Mathematics, Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee-IIT Roorkee, Haridwar Highway, Roorkee, Uttarakhand 247667, INDIA. e-mail: Om Tripathi: om_t@amsc.iitr.ac.in. e-mail: Sourav Kumar Sasmal: sourav.sasmal@amsc.iitr.ac.in. e-mail: Manil T. Mohan: maniltmohan@ma.iitr.ac.in, maniltmohan@gmail.com. *Corresponding author.
Om Tripathi1, Sourav Kumar Sasmal2*, and Manil T. Mohan3
Abstract.

We consider the following chemotaxis-growth system, featuring density-suppressed motility and a θ\theta-logistic growth term that incorporates a strong Allee effect:

{ut=Δ⁡(γ⁡(v)​u)+μ​u​(1−uθ)​(u−A),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δ​v−v+wβ,x∈Ω,t>0,wt=−δ​w+u,x∈Ω,t>0,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\begin{aligned} u_{t}&=\Delta(\gamma(v)u)+\mu u(1-u^{\theta})(u-A),&x\in\Omega,\quad t>0,\\ v_{t}&=\Delta v-v+w^{\beta},&x\in\Omega,\quad t>0,\\ w_{t}&=-\delta w+u,&x\in\Omega,\quad t>0,\end{aligned}}}\right.

subject to homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions in a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝd​(d≥2)\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}(d\geq 2) with smooth boundary. Here μ∈ℝ,δ,β>0,θ≥1\mu\in\mathbb{R},\delta,\beta>0,\theta\geq 1, and the positive motility function γ⁡(v)∈C3​([0,∞))\gamma(v)\in C^{3}([0,\infty)) fulfills γ′​(v)≤0\gamma^{\prime}(v)\leq 0 for all v≥0v\geq 0. The main objective of this paper is to establish the global existence and boundedness of classical solutions to the proposed problem. Our analysis combines the Schauder fixed point theorem for proving local-in-time existence with the extensibility criterion, fundamental energy estimates, Lp−L^{p}-bounds, the Gagliardo-Nirenberg interpolation inequality, Young’s inequality, semigroup estimates, and a Moser-type iteration scheme to derive uniform-in-time L∞−L^{\infty}-bounds, thereby ensuring global bounded classical solutions. More precisely, we establish that the chemotaxis-growth system admits a unique globally bounded classical solution whenever β<2​(θ+2)d\beta<\frac{2(\theta+2)}{d}. Furthermore, if the logarithmic derivative of the motility function is assumed to be uniformly bounded on [0,∞)[0,\infty), that is, γ′​(v)γ⁡(v)∈L∞​([0,∞))\frac{\gamma^{\prime}(v)}{\gamma(v)}\in L^{\infty}([0,\infty)), then the above restriction on β\beta can be weakened to β<d​(θ+1)+2​(θ+2)2​d\beta<\frac{d(\theta+1)+2(\theta+2)}{2d}, provided that θ>4−dd−2\theta>\frac{4-d}{d-2}.

Keywords: Global and local existence, uniqueness, chemotaxis, strong Allee effect, θ\theta-logistic growth, density suppressed motility.

MSC Classification 2020: 35B45, 35K57, 35Q92, 35A01, 92C17.

1. Introduction

Chemotaxis refers to the directed migration of biological entities toward or away from regions of varying chemical concentration. This phenomenon plays a significant role in various biological processes, including cell migration, aggregation, embryonic development, immune responses, and bacterial pattern formation. To mathematically describe such behavior, Keller and Segel proposed a pioneering class of chemotaxis models in their classical works [21, 22]. Since then, the Keller-Segel model has become one of the most extensively studied systems in mathematical biology and has attracted considerable attention over the past several decades. In a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} (d≥2)(d\geq 2) with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega, let u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) and v=v⁡(x,t),v=v(x,t), (x,t)∈Ω×[0,T](x,t)\in\Omega\times[0,T] denote the density of the cell population and the concentration of the chemoattractant, respectively. The classical Keller-Segel chemotaxis system with signal production, describing the movement of bacteria toward higher concentrations of self-produced chemical signals, is formulated as follows ([2]):

(1.1) {ut=∇⋅(φ(u,v)∇u−χ(u,v)u∇v)+f(u,v),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=DΔv+g(u,v),x∈Ω,t>0,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\begin{aligned} u_{t}&=\nabla\cdot\bigl(\varphi(u,v)\nabla u-\chi(u,v)u\nabla v\bigr)+f(u,v),\quad&&x\in\Omega,\;t>0,\\ v_{t}&=D\Delta v+g(u,v),\quad&&x\in\Omega,\;t>0,\end{aligned}}}\right.

where D>0D>0 is a constant. The function φ⁡(u,v)\varphi(u,v) denotes the diffusivity of the cells, while χ⁡(u,v)\chi(u,v) represents their chemotactic sensitivity. The cross-diffusion term −χ(u,v)u∇v-\chi(u,v)u\nabla v represents the chemotactic migration of bacteria in response to chemical concentration gradients, directing their movement toward regions of higher chemoattractant concentration. The function f⁡(u,v)f(u,v) models the net effect of bacterial proliferation and mortality, while g⁡(u,v)g(u,v) characterizes the generation and consumption of the chemical substance.

A comprehensive treatment of various chemotaxis processes can be found in [3, 14, 25, 28], and the references therein. Among the various Keller-Segel chemotaxis models, one of the most extensively studied classical parabolic-parabolic Keller-Segel system is

(1.2) {ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇v),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δv−v+u,x∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v),\quad&x\in\Omega,\;t>0,\\ v_{t}=\Delta v-v+u,\quad&x\in\Omega,\;t>0,\end{cases}

where χ>0\chi>0 is a positive fixed constant representing the chemotactic sensitivity. A remarkable feature of this system (1.2) is that the qualitative behavior of its solutions depends strongly on the spatial dimension. In the one-dimensional setting, Osaki and Yagi [35] established the global boundedness of solutions. In two-dimensional domains, Nagai et al. [34] proved the existence of globally bounded solutions provided that the initial cell mass satisfies ‖u0‖L1​(Ω)<4​πχ\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}<\frac{4\pi}{\chi}. Subsequently, this model has attracted considerable attention, leading to extensive studies on the existence, boundedness, and blow-up behavior of solutions. For comprehensive surveys and further developments, one can refer to Fujie and Senba [11], Horstmann [15, 16]. Moreover, Horstmann and Wang [17] showed that solutions may blow up in finite time whenever the initial cell mass satisfies ‖u0‖L1​(Ω)>4​πχ\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega)}>\frac{4\pi}{\chi}.

Several studies in mathematical biology have investigated chemotaxis models incorporating local sensing mechanisms [8, 29, 40]. In this mechanism, cells decrease motility at high concentrations of signaling molecules, which leads to a self-trapping effect that can induce aggregation and spatial patterns. Unlike the system (1.2), in the model (1.3) given below, the cellular diffusion rate and the chemotactic sensitivity are assumed to be nonlinear functions of the signal concentration in order to incorporate the effect of density-suppressed motility observed in bacterial populations. A typical model exhibiting this behavior is given by

(1.3) {ut=∇⋅(γ(v)u)+∇⋅(γ′(v)u∇u),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δv−v+u,x∈Ω,t>0,\begin{cases}\begin{aligned} u_{t}&=\nabla\cdot(\gamma(v)u)+\nabla\cdot(\gamma^{\prime}(v)u\nabla u),\quad&&x\in\Omega,\;t>0,\\ v_{t}&=\Delta v-v+u,\quad&&x\in\Omega,\;t>0,\end{aligned}\end{cases}

where u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) and v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) denote the density of the bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli) and the concentration of the signaling molecule acyl-homoserine lactone (AHL), respectively. Here, γ:[0,∞)→(0,∞)\gamma:[0,\infty)\to(0,\infty) denotes the cell motility function, which is assumed to be smooth and nonincreasing with respect to the chemical concentration vv. This assumption is biologically motivated by the observation that cell motility decreases as the chemical concentration increases.

The density-suppressed motility system has been extensively studied under various structural assumptions on the motility function γ\gamma. In particular, under the assumptions that γ\gamma is positive and uniformly bounded from above and below, with a bounded derivative, Tao and Winkler [46] established the existence of globally bounded classical solutions in bounded convex domains of two dimensions, as well as global weak solutions in higher-dimensional settings. Subsequently, Xiao and Jiang [52] extended these results by relaxing the boundedness requirement on γ′\gamma^{\prime} and established the global boundedness of classical solutions in bounded domains of arbitrary spatial dimension.

Further progress was made by Fujie and Senba [9], who established the global existence of bounded classical solutions under suitable smoothness and monotonicity assumptions on γ\gamma, together with the condition that γ⁡(s)→0\gamma(s)\to 0 as s→∞s\to\infty. Specific choices of the motility function have also been the subject of extensive investigation. In particular, for the algebraic motility function γ⁡(s)=c​s−k\gamma(s)=cs^{-k} with c,k>0c,k>0, the existence of global bounded classical solutions was established in [52], provided that cc is sufficiently small. In the prototype power-law case γ⁡(s)=s−k\gamma(s)=s^{-k}, Fujie and Senba [10] proved the global existence of bounded classical solutions for OPENk∈(0,2d−2CLOSE),d>2k\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,\frac{2}{d-2}}}\right),d>2. Moreover, when the motility function is chosen as γ⁡(s)=e−s\gamma(s)=e^{-s}, a critical-mass phenomenon was established in two-dimensional domains [9, 20].

Motivated by biological considerations, numerous studies have investigated the system (1.3) incorporating a logistic source and nonlinear production. The logistic source is commonly employed to model the proliferation and mortality of bacterial populations. Accordingly, the corresponding model is formulated as follows:

(1.4) {ut=∇⋅(γ(v)u)+∇⋅(γ′(v)u∇u)+f(u),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δv−v+uβ,x∈Ω,t>0.\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\begin{aligned} u_{t}&=\nabla\cdot(\gamma(v)u)+\nabla\cdot(\gamma^{\prime}(v)u\nabla u)+f(u),\quad&&x\in\Omega,\;t>0,\\ v_{t}&=\Delta v-v+u^{\beta},\quad&&x\in\Omega,\;t>0.\end{aligned}}}\right.

In the special case β=1\beta=1, the system with logistic growth f⁡(u)=μ​u​(1−u)f(u)=\mu u(1-u), μ>0\mu>0, was studied by Jin et al. [19] who proved the existence of globally bounded classical solutions in two-dimensional domains under the assumptions

γ∈C3​([0,∞)),γ>0,γ′≤0,lims→∞γ⁡(s)=0​ and ​lims→∞γ′​(s)γ⁡(s)​ exists.\gamma\in C^{3}([0,\infty)),\ \gamma>0,\ \gamma^{\prime}\leq 0,\ \lim_{s\to\infty}\gamma(s)=0\ \text{ and }\lim_{s\to\infty}\frac{\gamma^{\prime}(s)}{\gamma(s)}\ \text{ exists.}

Global classical solutions for dimensions d≥3d\geq 3 were obtained by Wang and Wang [49] under the boundedness of γ′\gamma^{\prime} and the sufficient largeness of the parameter μ\mu. Subsequently, Song et al. [37] considered the system (1.4) with β=1\beta=1 and a logistic growth term involving a strong Allee effect which is modeled as

(1.5) {ut=∇⋅(γ(v)u)+∇⋅(γ′(v)u∇u)+u(1−u)(u−A),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δv−v+u,x∈Ω,t>0,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\begin{aligned} u_{t}&=\nabla\cdot(\gamma(v)u)+\nabla\cdot(\gamma^{\prime}(v)u\nabla u)+u(1-u)(u-A),\quad&&x\in\Omega,\;t>0,\\ v_{t}&=\Delta v-v+u,\quad&&x\in\Omega,\;t>0,\end{aligned}}}\right.

where A∈(0,1)A\in(0,1) denotes the Allee threshold parameter. They proved the global existence and boundedness of classical solutions in spatial dimensions d≤3d\leq 3. The strong Allee effect refers to the phenomenon in which a population can persist and grow only if its density exceeds a critical value, known as the Allee threshold. Populations with densities below this threshold experience negative growth and are ultimately driven to extinction, whereas populations with densities above the threshold can survive and may converge to a positive equilibrium. The strong Allee effect occurs when low population density impairs essential biological processes, such as mate finding, cooperative behaviour, and predator avoidance [5, 26]. At bacterial level, to describe the interplay between chemotaxis and strong Allee effects, Mimura and Tsujikawa [23] proposed the following chemotaxis system:

{ut=∇⋅(d1∇u−χu∇B)+u(1−u)(u−A),x∈Ω,t>0,(d1∇u−χu∇B)⋅ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x)≥0,x∈Ω,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\begin{aligned} &u_{t}=\nabla\cdot(d_{1}\nabla u-\chi u\nabla B)+u(1-u)(u-A),\quad&&x\in\Omega,\;t>0,\\ &(d_{1}\nabla u-\chi u\nabla B)\cdot\nu=0,\quad&&x\in\partial\Omega,\;t>0,\\ &u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\geq 0,\quad&&x\in\Omega,\end{aligned}}}\right.

where BB represents a given environmental stimulus responsible for directed motion, and ν\nu denotes the outward unit normal vector on ∂Ω\partial\Omega. The study established the existence of multiple spike-type localized solutions under strong advection and analyzed their stability by examining the spectrum of the corresponding linearized eigenvalue problem.

In order to incorporate stronger density-dependent growth effects, several authors have considered chemotaxis systems with generalized logistic source terms in (1.4), where f⁡(u)=r​u−μ​uαf(u)=ru-\mu u^{\alpha} with r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R} and μ>0\mu>0. Such nonlinear growth terms provide a stronger damping effect that suppresses excessive cell aggregation, thereby playing an important role in proving the global existence and uniform boundedness of solutions. Under suitable assumptions on the motility function, γ\gamma, Lv and Wang [31] proved the existence of globally bounded classical solutions for α>max{d+22, 2}\alpha>\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\frac{d+2}{2},\,2}}\right\} for the system (1.4). Subsequently, Tao and Fang [41] investigated the case β>0\beta>0 and established the global boundedness of classical solutions whenever β<2​αd+2\beta<\frac{2\alpha}{d+2}. In addition, several other variants of chemotaxis systems with signal-dependent motility, including models incorporating signal absorption, have also been extensively studied [47, 51].

Conventionally, chemotaxis models assume that the chemoattractant is produced directly by the cellular population, as in the systems (1.1)-(1.4). However, this assumption is not suitable for certain biological processes in which the chemical signal is generated indirectly through intermediate substances. To capture such mechanisms, a variety of chemotaxis models with indirect signal production have been proposed and extensively investigated. One important application of these models arises in the mathematical description of the aggregation and dispersal of Mountain Pine Beetles (MPB) [39, 45]. A representative model is given by

(1.6) {ut=Δu−∇⋅(u∇v)+μu−μuα,x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δv−v+wβ,x∈Ω,t>0,wt=−δw+u,x∈Ω,t>0,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\begin{aligned} u_{t}&=\Delta u-\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v)+\mu u-\mu u^{\alpha},\quad&&x\in\Omega,\;t>0,\\ v_{t}&=\Delta v-v+w^{\beta},\quad&&x\in\Omega,\;t>0,\\ w_{t}&=-\delta w+u,\quad&&x\in\Omega,\;t>0,\end{aligned}}}\right.

where μ,δ,β>0\mu,\delta,\beta>0 and α>1\alpha>1. The variables uu, ww, and vv denote the densities of flying MPBs, nesting MPBs, and the beetle pheromone, respectively. For the case α=2\alpha=2 and β=1\beta=1, Hu and Tao [18] established the global existence and boundedness of classical solutions in three-dimensional domains. Subsequently, Li and Tao [27] extended this result to arbitrary spatial dimensions by proving the global existence of bounded classical solutions whenever α>d2\alpha>\frac{d}{2}. Motivated by these developments, several authors have further investigated the system (1.6) by incorporating signal-dependent (density-suppressed) motility of the form

(1.7) {ut=∇⋅(γ(v)u)−∇⋅(γ′(v)u∇u)+ru−μuα,x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δv−v+wβ,x∈Ω,t>0,wt=−δw+u,x∈Ω,t>0.\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\begin{aligned} u_{t}&=\nabla\cdot(\gamma(v)u)-\nabla\cdot(\gamma^{\prime}(v)u\nabla u)+ru-\mu u^{\alpha},\quad&&x\in\Omega,\;t>0,\\ v_{t}&=\Delta v-v+w^{\beta},\quad&&x\in\Omega,\;t>0,\\ w_{t}&=-\delta w+u,\quad&&x\in\Omega,\;t>0.\end{aligned}}}\right.

Recently, Lv and Wang [30] studied system (1.7) in the case β=1\beta=1 and α>1\alpha>1. By imposing suitable additional conditions on the motility function γ\gamma, they proved the global existence of bounded classical solutions whenever α>3​dd+2\alpha>\frac{3d}{d+2}.

1.1. Problem formulation and main results

Motivated by the ecological significance of the strong Allee effect in (1.5), we consider replacing the generalized logistic source term in the system (1.7) with a θ\theta-logistic growth term incorporating a strong Allee effect [4]. This formulation captures both nonlinear density-dependent regulation and the existence of a critical population threshold, leading to more realistic population dynamics and a stronger damping effect against excessive aggregation. Accordingly, we study the following chemotaxis system:

(1.8) {ut=Δ(γ(v)u)+μu(1−uθ)(u−A),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δv−v+wβ,x∈Ω,t>0,wt=−δw+u,x∈Ω,t>0,∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,u(x,0)=u0(x),v(x,0)=v0(x),w(x,0)=w0(x),x∈Ω,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\begin{aligned} &u_{t}=\Delta(\gamma(v)u)+\mu u(1-u^{\theta})(u-A),\quad&&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ &v_{t}=\Delta v-v+w^{\beta},\quad&&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ &w_{t}=-\delta w+u,\quad&&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ &\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0,\quad&&x\in\partial\Omega,\\ &u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\quad v(x,0)=v_{0}(x),\quad w(x,0)=w_{0}(x),\quad&&x\in\Omega,\end{aligned}}}\right.

in a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} (d≥2)(d\geq 2) with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega, assuming that ∂Ω\partial\Omega is of class C2+αC^{2+\alpha} for some 0<α<10<\alpha<1. Throughout this paper, we assume that the parameters μ∈ℝ\mu\in\mathbb{R}, β,δ>0\beta,\delta>0, A∈(0,1)A\in(0,1), and θ≥1\theta\geq 1. In addition, for the existence of local solutions, the initial data (u0,v0,w0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}) are assumed to satisfy

(1.9) {u0∈C0​(Ω¯),v0,w0∈C1​(Ω¯),u0,v0,w0≥0​and​u0≢0.\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\begin{aligned} &u_{0}\in C^{0}(\overline{\Omega}),\ v_{0},w_{0}\in C^{1}(\overline{\Omega}),\\ &u_{0},\,v_{0},\,w_{0}\geq 0\ \text{and}\ u_{0}\not\equiv 0.\end{aligned}}}\right.
Remark 1.1.

One may relax the conditions of the initial data in the following way also

{u0∈C0​(Ω¯),v0,w0∈W1,∞​(Ω),u0,v0,w0≥0​and​u0≢0.\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\begin{aligned} &u_{0}\in C^{0}(\overline{\Omega}),\ v_{0},w_{0}\in W^{1,\infty}({\Omega}),\\ &u_{0},\,v_{0},\,w_{0}\geq 0\ \text{and}\ u_{0}\not\equiv 0.\end{aligned}}}\right.

By the Sobolev embedding W1,∞​(Ω)↪C0​(Ω¯)W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow C^{0}(\overline{\Omega}), the above implies v0,w0∈C0​(Ω¯)v_{0},\,w_{0}\in C^{0}(\overline{\Omega}).

For the uniqueness of local solutions, we assume that the initial data satisfy the following:

(1.10) OPEN(u0,v0,w0)∈(C2+α​(Ω¯)CLOSE)3​ for some ​ 0<α<1,u0,v0≥0​ with ​u0≢0​ and\displaystyle(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C^{2+\alpha}(\overline{\Omega})}}\right)^{3}\ \text{ for some }\ 0<\alpha<1,\ u_{0},v_{0}\geq 0\text{ with }\ u_{0}\not\equiv 0\ \text{ and }
∂νu0=∂νv0=0​on ​∂Ω.\displaystyle\partial_{\nu}u_{0}=\partial_{\nu}v_{0}=0\ \text{on }\partial\Omega.

Moreover, we assume that the motility function satisfies

(1.11) γ(v)∈C3([0,∞)),γ(v)>0,γ′(v)<0 on [0,∞),and limv→∞γ(v)=0,\gamma(v)\in C^{3}([0,\infty)),\ \gamma(v)>0,\ \gamma^{\prime}(v)<0\ \text{ on }\ [0,\infty),\ \text{and }\ \lim_{v\to\infty}\gamma(v)=0,

with an extra assumption that

(1.12) limv→∞γ′​(v)γ⁡(v)​ exists.\lim_{v\to\infty}\frac{\gamma^{\prime}(v)}{\gamma(v)}\text{ exists}.

The primary aim of this work is to determine suitable conditions on the parameters θ\theta and β\beta that ensure the existence and uniqueness of globally bounded classical solutions to system (1.8). The principal results of this study are summarized below.

Theorem 1.1.

Let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} (d≥2)(d\geq 2) be a bounded domain with smooth boundary. Suppose that the initial data satisfy (1.9), with μ,β,δ>0\mu,\beta,\delta>0 and θ≥1\theta\geq 1. If the motility function satisfies (1.11) and β<2​(θ+2)d,\beta<\frac{2(\theta+2)}{d}, then problem (1.8) admits a globally bounded classical solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w). Moreover, there exists a constant C>0C>0, independent of tt, such that

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,∞​(Ω)+‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤C,for all ​t>0.\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|v(\cdot,t)\|_{W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)}+\|w(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq C,\ \text{for all }t>0.
Remark 1.2.

The global boundedness of classical solutions was established for the direct signal production system with the generalized logistic source term f⁡(u)=r​u−μ​uαf(u)=ru-\mu u^{\alpha}, under the condition β<2​αd+2\beta<\frac{2\alpha}{d+2} [41], which was later improved to β<2​αd\beta<\frac{2\alpha}{d} for the corresponding indirect signal production system [55]. In contrast, Theorem 1.1 proves global boundedness for a wider range of β\beta, highlighting the stronger damping effect of the θ\theta-logistic source term.

Under stronger assumptions on the motility function, we obtain the following result.

Theorem 1.2.

Let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} (d≥2)(d\geq 2) be a bounded domain with smooth boundary. Suppose that the initial data satisfy (1.9), with μ,β,δ>0\mu,\beta,\delta>0 and θ≥1\theta\geq 1. If the motility function satisfies both (1.11) and (1.12), then the condition imposed in Theorem 1.1 for the existence of globally bounded classical solutions can be relaxed to β<d​(θ+1)+2​(θ+2)2​d,\beta<\frac{d(\theta+1)+2(\theta+2)}{2d}, provided that θ>4−dd−2.\theta>\frac{4-d}{d-2}.

Remark 1.3.

In system (1.8), the parameter θ≥1\theta\geq 1 determines the strength of the density-dependent damping, while β\beta represents the production rate of vv. Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 demonstrate that the balance between these two effects is crucial when the damping induced by θ\theta is sufficiently strong relative to the production governed by β\beta, and the solution component uu remains uniformly bounded for all time.

1.2. Difficulties, approaches and novelties

In Section 2, the condition in Lemma 2.8 is repeatedly used in the analysis of the vv-equation; see, for instance, [19, 30, 41, 54, 55]. Nevertheless, the endpoint case m=∞m=\infty is not explicitly covered by the existing estimates. To address this issue, we extend the estimate from [50, Lemma 1.3], stated in Lemma 2.6(i), to the endpoint p=∞p=\infty. Since the original result does not include this endpoint, we provide a separate proof in Lemma 2.7. This extension allows us to rigorously apply the corresponding estimate in the case m=∞m=\infty. Consequently, we obtain a constant C>0C>0 such that ‖∇v‖L∞​(Ω)≤C\|\nabla v\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq C whenever β<kd​with​β≤k\beta<\frac{k}{d}\ \text{with}\ \beta\leq k in Lemma 2.8.

To the best of our knowledge, the regularity assumptions imposed on the initial data for establishing the existence and uniqueness of local solutions to (1.8) have not been explicitly characterized in the existing literature [19, 30, 37, 55] on chemotaxis systems with density-suppressed motility and indirect signal production. The construction of local classical solutions is, however, nontrivial, as the initial data prescribed in (1.9) do not possess sufficient regularity to permit a direct application of the abstract parabolic theory developed in [24] within a Schauder fixed-point framework. To address this issue, we approximate the given initial data (1.9) by a sequence of smoother functions that satisfy the appropriate compatibility conditions such that {(u0n,v0n,w0n)}n∈ℕ∈(C2+α​(Ω¯))3, 0<α<1,with​∂νu0n=∂νv0n=0​on ​∂Ω\{(u_{0}^{n},v_{0}^{n},w_{0}^{n})\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in\bigl(C^{2+\alpha}(\overline{\Omega})\bigr)^{3},\ 0<\alpha<1,\ \text{with}\ \partial_{\nu}u_{0}^{n}=\partial_{\nu}v_{0}^{n}=0\ \text{on }\partial\Omega. Using the closed, bounded, and convex set in the underlying Banach space introduced for the fixed-point argument in Section 3, we establish the necessary parabolic Hölder estimates for the local solutions associated with the regularized initial data. These estimates allow us to construct a sequence of local approximating solutions to (1.8). We then exploit the compactness of the relevant parabolic Hölder embeddings to extract a subsequence that converges strongly in the required function spaces. This convergence enables us to pass to the limit in the approximating problem and thereby obtain the desired local solution of (1.8).

The construction of local classical solutions to (1.8) requires some additional care, mainly due to the possibility that the motility function γ\gamma may vanish, thereby causing degeneracy in the diffusion term of the uu-equation. Consequently, the standard theory for uniformly parabolic equations is not directly applicable. To handle this degeneracy, we introduce an appropriate cut-off and replace γ\gamma with a truncated motility function γ^\widehat{\gamma} in (3.7) that remains uniformly positive.

Another difficulty arises in establishing uniqueness of local solutions for the initial data specified in (1.9). The uniqueness argument requires sufficient regularity of (u,v,w)(u,v,w) on Ω×[0,Tmax)\Omega\times[0,T_{\max}), in particular the regularity stated in (3.1) and (3.34). Under the weaker assumptions imposed on the initial data in (1.9), the regularity, u∈L∞​([0,Tmax),W1,∞​(Ω)),u\in L^{\infty}\big([0,T_{\max});W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)\big), is not immediately available. Therefore, we establish uniqueness separately for initial data satisfying the stronger regularity assumptions in (1.10), for which the corresponding solution possesses the regularity required by Theorem 3.2.

The sublinear production term wβw^{\beta} in the vv-equation introduces a further complication, making the analysis more involved than in the linear case β=1\beta=1 considered in [19, 37]. When 0<β<10<\beta<1, the function w↦wβw\mapsto w^{\beta} is not globally Lipschitz continuous, which creates difficulties in verifying the continuity of the fixed-point operator. This issue is addressed through suitable estimates based on the inequality (2.1). For β≥1\beta\geq 1, on the other hand, the nonlinear term can be controlled more directly by means of the inequality (2.2). In addition, for 0<β<10<\beta<1, the uniqueness argument requires the strict positivity of w0w_{0} in order to obtain a positive lower bound for wiw_{i}, whereas the weaker assumption w0≥0w_{0}\geq 0 is sufficient when β≥1\beta\geq 1. These distinctions motivate treating the existence and uniqueness of local classical solutions separately in the two parameter regimes.

A further significant challenge in establishing the global existence of classical solutions to system (1.8) arises from the density-suppressed motility mechanism under the assumption γ′​(v)≤0\gamma^{\prime}(v)\leq 0. In contrast to many classical chemotaxis and reaction-diffusion models, the motility function γ⁡(v)\gamma(v) is not assumed to be bounded away from zero, which may cause the diffusion in the uu-equation to become degenerate. As a result, several standard techniques commonly used to prove the global existence and boundedness of solutions cannot be applied directly and require substantial modification. So, for this purpose, we have established the higher regularity of vv in Lemma 4.3, for attaining the lower bound on γ\gamma under the condition β<2​(θ+2)d\beta<\frac{2(\theta+2)}{d}. For lower-dimensional cases under assumptions (1.11) and (1.12), the analysis is comparatively simpler.

In Section 4, for d≥2d\geq 2, we develop the analysis under the sole structural assumption (1.11) on the motility function. We first establish a uniform-in-time upper bound for vv. In particular, Lemma 2.18 yields a W1,qW^{1,q}-estimate for vv with q>dq>d, which provides the regularity needed to derive an LpL^{p}-bound for uu, with p>2p>2 sufficiently large, as shown in Lemma 4.4. Subsequently, by combining the Gagliardo–Nirenberg interpolation inequality with the Moser iteration procedure in Lemma 4.5, we upgrade this LpL^{p}-estimate to a uniform L∞L^{\infty}-bound for uu. This uniform-in-time bound on uu is a key ingredient in establishing the global existence of classical solutions stated in Theorem 1.1.

Moreover, when the motility function satisfies the additional assumption (1.12), the approach developed in Section 5 avoids the need for higher-order regularity estimates for vv. Instead, we establish a coupled differential inequality involving ∫Ωup\int_{\Omega}u^{p}, ∫Ω|∇v|2​q\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{2q}, and ∫Ωwp\int_{\Omega}w^{p} in Lemma 5.4, valid for all t∈(0,Tmax)t\in(0,T_{\max}). The main challenge is the presence of nonlinear terms of the form ∫Ω|∇v|χi\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{\chi_{i}}, where the exponents χi\chi_{i} depend on pp, qq, β\beta, and θ\theta. To control these terms, we choose pp and qq appropriately according to the conditions in Lemma 5.5. The Gagliardo-Nirenberg interpolation inequality then allows us to estimate each ∫Ω|∇v|χi\int_{\Omega}|\nabla v|^{\chi_{i}} in terms of the quantities appearing in the differential inequality, which ultimately yields the required LpL^{p}-bound for uu. Once this estimate is established, the conditions on qq given in Lemma 5.5 ensure that q>d2q>\frac{d}{2} for some p>p∗p>p* defined in (5.37). Consequently, the Sobolev embedding yields the uniform estimate ‖v‖L∞​(Ω)≤C\|v\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq C. The remainder of the argument can then be carried out in a manner analogous to the proof of Theorem 1.1, ultimately leading to the global boundedness of the classical solutions.

It is worth highlighting that our analysis is performed in the presence of a θ\theta-logistic growth term incorporating a strong Allee effect. The resulting nonlinear damping mechanism is instrumental in deriving the higher-order estimates needed for the global existence results. To the best of our knowledge, global solvability for chemotaxis systems that simultaneously involve density-suppressed motility, indirectly produced nonlinear signals, and θ\theta-logistic growth with a strong Allee effect has not been studied in the existing literature. Our results therefore extend the current theory by identifying admissible ranges of the parameter β\beta for which the damping generated by the θ\theta-logistic term is sufficiently strong to compensate for the destabilizing effects arising from density-suppressed motility and nonlinear signal production.

1.3. Organization of the paper

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the basic preliminaries, including the functional spaces, auxiliary lemmas, and technical tools that will be used throughout the paper. In Section 3, we establish the local existence and uniqueness of classical solutions. Section 4 is devoted to the global boundedness of classical solutions under assumption (1.11) on the motility function. To avoid the additional restrictions imposed in earlier works [19, 30, 37], we first derive an appropriate Lθ+2L^{\theta+2} estimate for ww in Lemma 4.2. This estimate is then combined with Neumann heat semigroup estimates to establish LqL^{q}-bounds for ∇v\nabla v and the uniform-in-time boundedness of vv in Lemma 4.3. The resulting regularity of vv enables us to derive LpL^{p}-estimates for uu in Lemma 4.4. Finally, these estimates are incorporated into the Alikakos–Moser iteration scheme to obtain the uniform-in-time boundedness of uu, thereby completing the proof of Theorem 1.1.

In Section 5, we investigate the global boundedness of classical solutions under the combined assumptions (1.11) and (1.12). We begin by establishing a series of a priori estimates for the solution, as presented in Lemmas 5.1-5.4. These estimates form the basis for deriving an LpL^{p}-estimate of uu in Lemma 5.6, where a suitable admissible range of the parameter β\beta is identified through Lemma 5.5. With these estimates in hand, the proof of Theorem 1.2 follows by adapting the arguments developed in Section 4 for uniform-in-time bound of uu.

3. Local existence and uniqueness

In this section, we establish the local existence and uniqueness of classical solutions to system (1.8). The main difficulty arises from the possible degeneracy of the motility function, which hinders the direct application of the classical theory for uniformly parabolic equations. To overcome this difficulty, we introduce a suitable cut-off function and construct an approximate uniformly parabolic system. We then employ classical parabolic regularity theory to derive the parabolic Hölder estimates required to verify the self-mapping property of the associated fixed-point operator. The existence of local classical solutions is obtained by applying the Schauder fixed-point theorem, while uniqueness follows from suitable a priori estimates.

Our proof is based on the framework developed in [19, Lemma 2.1] and the approach adopted in [44, Section 2]. However, several modifications are required to deal with the additional difficulties posed by the present system.

Theorem 3.1.

Let Ω⊂ℝd\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} (d≥2)(d\geq 2) be a bounded domain with smooth boundary, and let μ,β,δ>0\mu,\beta,\delta>0, r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R}, and θ≥1\theta\geq 1. If the initial data fullfill (1.9) and that the motility function satisfies hypothesis (1.11), then there exist Tmax∈(0,∞]T_{\max}\in(0,\infty] and a triple of non-negative functions (u,v,w)(u,v,w) satisfying

(3.1) {u∈C0​(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,Tmax)),v∈C0​(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,Tmax))∩L∞​([0,Tmax),W1,∞​(Ω)),w∈C0,1​(Ω¯×[0,Tmax)),\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\begin{aligned} u&\in C^{0}\big(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T_{\max})\big)\cap C^{2,1}\big(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,T_{\max})\big),\\[5.69054pt] v&\in C^{0}\big(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T_{\max})\big)\cap C^{2,1}\big(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,T_{\max})\big)\cap L^{\infty}\big([0,T_{\max});W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)\big),\\[5.69054pt] w&\in C^{0,1}\big(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T_{\max})\big),\end{aligned}}}\right.

which solves (1.8) in the classical sense. Moreover, if Tmax<∞T_{\max}<\infty, then it follows that

(3.2) lim supt→Tmax‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)=∞.\displaystyle\limsup_{t\to T_{\max}}\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}=\infty.
Proof.

Since the initial data (1.9) do not possess sufficient regularity required to apply the abstract results from [24], we first approximate them by a sequence of smoother functions. Specifically, for the non-negative initial data (u0,v0,w0)∈C0​(Ω¯)×C1​(Ω¯)×C1​(Ω¯)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in C^{0}(\overline{\Omega})\times C^{1}(\overline{\Omega})\times C^{1}(\overline{\Omega}), there exists a sequence

Having established the local existence of classical solutions satisfying (3.1), we now turn to their uniqueness. The previous theorem guarantees the existence of at least one local classical solution for lower regularity initial data satisfying

(3.31) u∈C2+l4, 1+l42​(Ω¯×[ε,Tmax)),v∈C2+l3, 1+l32​(Ω¯×[ε,Tmax)),\displaystyle u\in C^{2+l_{4},\,1+\frac{l_{4}}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[\varepsilon,T_{\max})),\ v\in C^{2+l_{3},\,1+\frac{l_{3}}{2}}(\overline{\Omega}\times[\varepsilon,T_{\max})),

Remark 3.1.

The initial data are regularized according to (3.3) in order to invoke the abstract parabolic theory [24, Theorem 6.1, Chapter V, p. 452]. The resulting regularity of uu and vv plays a key role in showing the continuity of the associated fixed-point map, thereby allowing the Schauder fixed-point theorem to be applied to construct local classical solutions with the regularity stated in (3.1). In the absence of this regularization, the classical parabolic regularity in (3.31) alone does not yield the L∞​(Ω×(0,T))L^{\infty}(\Omega\times(0,T)) bound required for g1g_{1}. Consequently, the parabolic LpL^{p}-regularity estimate in (3.24) cannot be applied directly.

We shall now show that, under a stronger regularity assumption on the initial data given in (3.3), the corresponding local classical solution satisfying (3.1) is unique.

Before proving Theorem 1.2, we compare the restrictions on β\beta arising from the preceding results. Theorem 1.1 guarantees the global existence of solutions to (1.8) under the condition β<2​(θ+2)d\beta<\frac{2(\theta+2)}{d}, whereas Lemma 5.6 requires β<d​(θ+1)+2​(θ+2)2​d\beta<\frac{d(\theta+1)+2(\theta+2)}{2d}. Hence, in this parameter regime, the restriction imposed by Theorem 1.1 is more restrictive than that of Lemma 5.6.

6. Conclusion and future directions

In this work, we investigated the global existence and uniqueness of globally bounded classical solutions to system (1.8). We first established the local existence and uniqueness of classical solutions in Section 3 by applying the Schauder fixed point theorem together with suitable a priori estimates, after replacing the motility function with an appropriate cutoff function. Subsequently, in Section 4, assuming only condition (1.11) on the motility function, we proved the global existence of classical solutions under the condition β<2​(θ+2)d\beta<\frac{2(\theta+2)}{d}. Furthermore, by additionally imposing the condition (1.12), we significantly enlarged the admissible range of the parameter β\beta and established global existence under the condition β<d​(θ+1)+2​(θ+2)2​d\beta<\frac{d(\theta+1)+2(\theta+2)}{2d} whenever θ>4−dd−2\theta>\frac{4-d}{d-2}.

Although the present work establishes the global existence and uniqueness of classical solutions, several challenging questions remain open. A natural continuation of this work is to investigate the large-time behavior of solutions through the construction of an appropriate Lyapunov functional for sufficiently large values of μ\mu, following the approach developed in [19, 55], which may yield further insight into the asymptotic dynamics of the system. Independently, it would also be worthwhile to examine the existence and stability of nonconstant steady-state solutions, as investigated in [37] for the case θ=1\theta=1. Owing to the strong coupling effects and nonlinearities inherent in the system, both directions are expected to require considerably more delicate analytical arguments than those developed in the present work.
